summary: This workflow calculates claim savings by joining claims, benchmarks, and case data, computing a running savings total per member, flagging top savers, and summarizing by program into four output files. It scores 9/10, the highest difficulty band, mainly because it uses a Python tool [13] with no SQL equivalent and calls an external macro [16] whose logic must be assessed separately. Several other pieces (RegEx [3], Multi-Row Formula [12]) also require rewriting as different SQL constructs.

key_components.description: Loads claims, benchmarks, and case data from CSV and joins them on procedure code and case ID.
Cleans and converts amount fields, parses a note field with a regular expression, and calculates allowed and savings amounts.
Sorts records by member and date, then computes a running savings total per member row by row.
Runs a Python script that flags claims in the top 10% of savings as 'top_saver'.
Summarizes savings by program via a macro, and writes out four separate result files.

risks.title: Python tool has no Redshift equivalent
risks.detail: The Python step [13] computes a 'top_saver' flag using a statistical quantile calculation; Redshift has no built-in Python execution (and Python UDFs are being discontinued), so this logic must be rewritten in SQL (e.g. using PERCENTILE_CONT) or run outside Redshift.

risks.title: Macro logic is in a separate file
risks.detail: The Macro [16] (wf4_program_summary.yxmc) contains logic not visible in this workflow file; it must be opened and assessed on its own before the program summary step can be migrated.

risks.title: Unmatched join records used downstream
risks.detail: The Join [6] passes its unmatched (left) output to a separate output file; this needs a dedicated LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right_key IS NULL query rather than a single join.

risks.title: RegEx translation differences
risks.detail: The RegEx tool [3] is case-insensitive, extracts a capture group, and uses Perl-style patterns; Redshift's REGEXP_SUBSTR is case-sensitive and POSIX-based by default, so the 'i', 'e', and 'p' parameters must be added and the result verified.

risks.title: Running total needs window function with explicit frame
risks.detail: The Multi-Row Formula [12] builds a running total by referencing the prior row; in Redshift this becomes a SUM() OVER (...) window function, which requires an explicit frame clause to behave the same way.

risks.title: Text-to-number conversion may fail on bad data
risks.detail: Currency text (e.g. '$', commas) is stripped before converting to numbers [2], and another conversion happens in [8]; in Redshift, any value that isn't a valid number after cleaning will cause the whole query to fail, unlike Alteryx's more tolerant handling.

next_steps: Open and analyze the macro file wf4_program_summary.yxmc separately, since its logic is not in this workflow.
Decide how to replace the Python top_saver calculation [13] in SQL (e.g. PERCENTILE_CONT) or plan to run it outside Redshift.
Test the RegEx pattern [3] in Redshift with the 'i', 'e', and 'p' parameters to confirm it matches Alteryx's output.
Rewrite the running savings calculation [12] as a window function with an explicit frame clause and validate results row by row.
Audit the allowed_amount and benchmark_cost fields for all currency formats to ensure cleaning logic [2, 8] covers every case before casting.
Build the unmatched-claims query [6] as a separate LEFT JOIN ... WHERE IS NULL statement and confirm row counts match the original output.
